newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia Wheat - Concern over subsidy war.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia Wheat - Concern over subsidy war.

text.p: Concern that the United States will retaliate against a decision by the European Union (EU) to sell subsidised wheat is overshadowing the Australian market.

Closely-watched January 1997 wheat ended last week 50 cents lower at A$163.00 a tonne on modest volume, attributed to book squaring ahead of USDA quarterly wheat stock figures due out on later on Monday.
Price flucuations last week were attributed to spread trading the nearby months, with the Australian Wheat Board cutting its pool price estimate A$10.00 to A$195.00 a tonne FOB.
As a result, nearby contracts by Friday had all settled lower on the week.
A breakout of a U.S.-EU subsidy war would probably firm up prices between the combatants, while making Australian wheat less attractive in price to such key buyers as China.
The North Dakota Wheat Commission said on Thursday the United States needed Export Enhancement Program (EEP) subsidies to counter the European Union's Actions.
But whether the U.S. would actually impose its own subsidies -- more than likely in the form of EEP -- is debatable given that U.S. wheat is running above export parity.

Fearful that such a scenario may unfold, however, some brokers are encouraging Australian growers to take out put options, as the U.S. and Australian markets would probably move in opposite directions.
"The U.S. is keeping its EEP budget and could retaliate, basically shooting EEP bullets at Europe, and Australia will get caught in the cross-fire," said a grains analyst.
The last time the U.S. imposed EEP subisides was nearly two years ago at the height of the last trade war. But there may be less reason for the U.S. to react this time around.

"U.S. supply-demand is fairly tight, so there will be a significantly smaller quantity of U.S. wheat going into the export market this year," said a grains trader. "Domestic U.S. wheat prices are reflecting that tightness."
